endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: requires such reviews include human examination of patient records prior to a care denial.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Human oversight is vital for ensuring fairness in the prior authorization process.

evidence.title: Role-Prompting in Frontier Large Language Models Influences Clinical Reasoning in Complex Medical Cases
evidence.effect: Insurer role produced systematic denial; alignment fell 50% for GPT-5.4, 45% for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 10.5% for Opus 4.6.
evidence.quote: Stakeholder role-prompting fundamentally alters clinical decisions and ethical value frameworks of frontier LLMs, with the insurer role producing systematic denial of physician-endorsed, patient-preferred treatments.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (25 cases x 3 roles x 3 runs x 3 models)

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether individualized human clinical review with override ability reduces wrongful AI-assisted denials of care, claims, or prior authorization. One simulation study found that large language models assigned an insurer role denied guideline-endorsed treatments more often, which suggests the hazard exists, and two guidance documents endorse human review.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, so certainty about its effect cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study used 675 simulated model responses to 25 vignettes. It shows that role framing shifted model outputs toward denial. It does not measure whether a human reviewer would catch or reverse those denials.

When prompted as an insurer, models showed alignment with endorsed treatments falling 50% for GPT-5.4, 45% for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 10.5% for Opus 4.6. This suggests an unreviewed output could deny appropriate care. Whether human review intercepts these errors, or whether reviewers defer to the model, has not been studied.

Two sources endorse the practice. The augmented intelligence principles state it as a requirement that reviewers examine patient records before a denial, and the CHAI guide describes human oversight as necessary for fairness in prior authorization. These endorsements reflect expert consensus rather than tested outcomes.

The hazard study indicates that the same model can reach different conclusions depending on whose interests it is told to represent. Patients facing a denial may reasonably expect a clinician to have read their record, and the endorsing guidance supports that expectation, though no study shows how often review changes the decision.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI-assisted denial workflows with and without individualized clinician review, measuring overturn rates, appeal outcomes, time to care, reviewer agreement with model outputs, and reviewer workload in live payer operations.
commentary.underserved_note: The only study was an offline vignette simulation that did not report patient population characteristics, and no study tested the practice in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether human review would reduce wrongful denials for these groups, who may have fewer resources to pursue appeals.
